CODE CHECKS REVIEW, 1.24.36 (commit ca62870; 1.24.35 = 8cb3281 beside it)
Reviewer: an agent that did not write the change. tests/code_checks_1236.js and tests/fixtures/givens_review_1236/ were
not read. Every case here is the reviewer's own.

Replay: node tests/fixtures/code_checks_review_1236/replay.js [inner.html]   (about 16 s; output in run_ca62870.txt)
src/lantern.inner.html at the time of the run is byte-identical to ca62870's (sha256 45450b13...617e).

SUMMARY
338 cases: 276 AGREE, 62 DISAGREE (29 high, 20 medium, 13 low).
- 202 control circuits (cases_circuits.js): 145 right ones that must pass, 49 wrong ones that must go back with a line
  that works when copied, 8 misses and false claims. 70 questions for pick() (cases_pick.js). 66 others (cases_misc.js):
  the view and the saved choice, Lantern.store throwing or missing, module drops, the bench guard, saved replies,
  Lantern's own givens and stations, what the correction (fixText) looks like copied, the code's form, the references.
- What works well: every wrong circuit of the kinds the module names, written on the switch's own line, is caught, and its "Write it" line, copied as it
  stands (with fixText's full stop after it), builds and draws right in every spelling tried. The view, the saved
  choice, store failures, module drops, ES5/ASCII/regex rules, the bench prompts and all 2,105 saved replies are clean.
  Every reference Lantern names matches the title on the page read.
- What does not: rule 7. The cut-out check acts on words that say "high" or "low" and "cut" without asking what the
  switch's OUTPUT is, so alarms, fans, relief and dump valves, unloaders, heaters that run on cold, and trip timers
  are sent back and told to write the opposite. Three parsing slips add more (a minus sign dropped, "min" read as
  minimum, "freezer" read as freeze). And the checks read the switch's own line, not the contact as drawn, so a
  contact named on the coil's line (the HINT's own form) is judged the wrong way round. All 30 right circuits sent
  back (28 high, 2 medium) built and drew as written on 1.24.35 (the same cases run against 8cb3281): each is a
  regression of this change.

======================================================================================================================
HIGH (right circuits sent back, or the line handed back draws a wrong circuit)
======================================================================================================================
Each "sent back" below tells the model to write the opposite contact. A model that copies the line draws a circuit
that runs the output only when it should not.

H1. Over/trip/safety/protect words with an output that is not the thing cut out.            [10 cases]
  R-alarm-02 "high pressure trip alarm" -> CR1 "alarm relay"
  R-alarm-03 "over temperature alarm"   -> CR1 "alarm relay"
  R-alarm-06 "overfill alarm"           -> CR1 "alarm relay"
  R-alarm-07 "high pressure safety alarm" -> TR1 (an alarm delay timer, horn on TR1)
  R-fan-03 "over temperature" -> M1 "cabinet cooling fan";  R-fan-04 "overheat" -> M1 "exhaust fan";
  R-fan-09 "overheat" -> CR1 "fan relay";  R-fan-12 "high temperature protection" -> M1 "cabinet fan"
  R-fill-07 "overfill" -> SOL1 "dump valve";  R-sol-01 "over pressure relief" -> SOL1 "relief valve"
  Seen: "... is a high cut-out written normally open: CR1 would run only while the pressure is above it ... Write it:
  pressure PS1 CR1 nc ...". Right: each of these outputs must come ON as the quantity rises past the switch, so
  written without nc (closes on rise) is right; nc would sound the alarm, run the fan, open the relief only while
  things are normal. Why it happens: OVERW (over-pressure, over-temp, overheat, overfill) is read as a high cut-out
  with no cut word at all, and "trip", "safety", "protect\w*" are cut words; the only outputs left alone are lamps and
  horns (RUNS = coil, timer, solenoid, alternator). Rule 7 asks what else it can be: the output's own label (alarm,
  fan, relief, dump, unloader, a timer) answers. An alarm relay is the commonest way an alarm is wired to a horn and a
  light at once.

H2. Low and freeze words where the output runs on the low side by design.                    [8 cases]
  R-heat-10 "frost stat" nc -> M1 "boiler relay" (question: UK house; sent back in IEC practice)
  R-heat-11 "freeze protection" nc -> M1 "heat trace contactor";  R-heat-16 "frost protection" nc -> "tank heater"
  R-heat-19 "low limit" nc -> CR1 "low limit call" (a boiler aquastat's low limit, which fires the burner as the
            water cools)
  R-heat-12 "freezer defrost termination" nc -> M2 "defrost heaters"
  R-ref-13 "loss of oil pressure" nc -> TR1 "90 s";  R-ref-14 "low oil pressure safety" nc -> TR1 "120 s"
            (a refrigeration oil safety: the switch is closed while the oil pressure is low and runs the trip timer;
            the timer's closed contact drops the compressor)
  R-alarm-08 "low water cut-off alarm" nc -> CR2 "alarm relay" (the LWCO's alarm contact)
  Seen: "is a low cut-out written normally closed: M1 would run only while the temperature is below it ... Write it:
  temp TS1 M1 \"frost stat\"". Right: each of these outputs must run below the setting, which is exactly what the
  message calls wrong. Why: LOWSELF (freeze\w*, frost\w*, loss of, dry run, no flow) makes a low cut-out with no cut
  word and whatever the output; \bfreeze\w* also matches "freezer"; "low limit" is acted on in both of its senses
  (an air handler's freeze stat opens on fall -- W-lowlimit-47, rightly caught -- and a boiler's low limit closes on
  fall). By rule 7 the name alone is not sure.

H3. Cut-in/cut-out numbers read without their minus sign.                                     [2 cases]
  R-ref-10 "cut-in -12 C cut-out -18 C" (freezer), R-ref-11 "cut-in 5 F, cut-out -10 F"
  Seen: read as a HIGH cut-out (18 > 12, 10 > 5) and sent back to be written nc. Right: the cut-out is below the
  cut-in, a cooling stat that closes on rise, written without nc. The regexes in way() are
  /\bcut[\s-]?in\b\D{0,8}(\d+...)/ and the same for cut-out: \D{0,8} swallows the "-".

H4. "min" (minutes) read as minimum.                                                           [1 case]
  R-air-04 air compressor, pressure PS1 M1 nc "cut-out, restart after 3 min"
  Seen: read as a LOW cut-out (LOWW has \bmin\b) and told to take the nc off: the compressor would then run only above
  its cut-out. Right: nc, as written (the AIRQ default alone would have called it high and kept it).

H5. On an air compressor, well, booster or jet pump, every pressure "cut-out" is taken as the high one.   [5 cases]
  R-air-06 "oil pressure cut-out" (low oil pressure stops the compressor)
  R-pump-05 "dry well cut-off" (a well pump's low pressure cut-off)
  R-pump-06 "suction cut-out" (a booster's low suction cut-out)
  R-air-03 "unloads at cut-out" -> SOL1 "unloader";  R-air-10 "at cut-out" -> TR1 (an auto-stop idle timer)
  Seen: "is a high cut-out written normally open ... Write it: ... nc". Right: the first three cut out on LOW
  pressure (written without nc); the last two energise their output as the pressure reaches cut-out (written without
  nc). The AIRQ default (label says cut-out, neither high nor low, question names one of these machines) has no "what
  else could it be" step: the oil, suction, dry, unload words, or an output that is not the motor's coil, say it is
  another switch. (R-pump-11 "pump protection cut-out", the same path, is listed medium: its direction is unsure.)

H6. A contact named on the coil's line is judged by the switch's own line.                    [3 cases]
  W-coilnc-22 pressure PS1 "high pressure cut-out" + coil M1 PS1 nc "compressor contactor"
  W-coiloff-24 temp TS1 "high limit" + coil M1 TS1 off "burner"
  Seen: AI_CONTROL draws PS1 / TS1 normally CLOSED (the coil's nc or off turns the switch over: circuit(), "nc:
  rf.nc ? !d.nc : !!d.nc"), which is right, and the check sends it back as "written normally open" because it reads
  it.nc from the switch's own line.
  W-coilnc-22b: the line handed back, "pressure PS1 nc \"high pressure cut-out\"", copied as it stands with the coil's
  line unchanged, is drawn OPEN (turned over twice), passes, and is listed under the drawing as "PS1 opens as the
  pressure rises -- NFPA 79, exceeding operating limits". The fix makes a right circuit wrong and certifies it.
  The HINT teaches this form ("coil CR3 M1 off -- while M1 is off"), so a small model may write it. The check already
  walks the rungs (inR); judging the element as drawn there (its nc in c.rungs) would see what Lantern draws, and the
  line handed back would then have to be the coil's line (or say to take the nc off it).

======================================================================================================================
MEDIUM (clear misses, false "checked" claims, ambiguous names acted on, the practice chosen wrongly)
======================================================================================================================
M1. A stop shown as "normally closed" (or a cut-out as opening the right way) under a drawing where it is not.
  M-stopno-05 "stop PB1 M1 no", M-stopno-06 "stop PB1 M1 normally open": drawn OPEN (a hold-to-run), and listed
      "the stop normally closed -- NFPA 79, control functions in the event of failure". control-drawn counts every pb
      in r.stops without looking at nc.
  M-olno-07 "overload OL1 M1 no": drawn OPEN (the motor runs only with the overload tripped), listed "the overload
      OL1 on M1 -- NEC Article 430, Part III".
  M-dblnc-04 (nc on both the switch's and the coil's line) and M-lowcoil-08 (float FS1 "low water cut-off" + coil M1
      FS1 nc): drawn the wrong way round, listed "PS1 opens as the pressure rises" / "FS1 opens as the water falls".
  These drawings are as 1.24.35 drew them; what is new is a "Checked to US practice (NEC and NFPA 79)" stamp under a
  wrong drawing, which a person with nobody to ask will trust. They are listed medium as misses; they could fairly be
  read as high. The kept items should be read from what is drawn (nc in c.rungs), and the stop and overload written
  open sent back with their line.
M2. M-stop-02 "button PB1 M1 stop" (the name unquoted): drawn as a second start (as on 1.24.35), not caught -- the
  check reads only a quoted label -- and the line under it says "the stop normally closed" (of the stop Lantern
  added for the seal).
M3. An emergency stop handed back as an ordinary stop. W-stop-11 button PB1 M1 "emergency stop", W-estop-26 button ES1
  M1 "e-stop" (each beside a start): the line is "stop PB1 M1 \"emergency stop\"", drawn as a stop in M1's rung only,
  not listed as the emergency stop. Lantern's own line for one is "estop PB1" (drawn in L1 ahead of every rung).
M4. Ambiguous names acted on: R-sump-04 a sump's "high level safety" float that starts the pump (the question says so),
  sent back to be written nc; R-pump-11 a well pump's "pump protection cut-out" (a pump saver cuts out on LOW
  pressure), sent back as a high cut-out.
M5. pick() chooses the wrong practice (named in the line to the model and under the drawing; the rule itself is the
  same in both codes, so the line handed back is still right):
  - P-12 "a house in New England" -> IEC (\bengland\b); P-11 "the pump station on India Street" -> IEC (\bindia\b).
  - Adjectives are not read: P-21 European, P-22 German, P-46 Australian, P-47 Italian -> the saved choice / US.
    (SAYS_US reads "american" and "canadian"; SAYS_IEC reads only the country nouns, and "european" only with
    "union".)
  - P-17 "must be UL listed" with IEC saved -> IEC (only "UL 508A" is read); P-18 "a CE marked machine" -> US.
  - P-26 "South America", P-62 "Latin American" -> US (\bamerica\b, \bamerican\b), over the saved IEC.

======================================================================================================================
LOW
======================================================================================================================
- M-hp-01 "HP cut-out" (the refrigeration trade's high pressure cut-out) not read as high; M-start-03 a start button
  named "stop" drawn as a start. Rule 7 lets both be.
- pick(): P-09 "SHOW US ... 400 V" in capitals -> US (the pronoun read as the country); P-20 "Redraw this NEC starter
  to IEC 60204-1" -> US (both named: saved/US); P-24 "120/240 V" not read as US; P-28 "Poland Spring plant in Maine"
  and P-53 "Norway, Maine" -> IEC; P-31 "U.K." with full stops not read; P-44 "a UK house with a US-made compressor"
  -> US; P-45 "ISO 13849" alone -> IEC (used under both); P-54 "400 V motor in the USA" with IEC saved -> IEC (both
  named; the place should win over the voltage).
- T-08 the correction says "water" for every float ("M1 would run only while the water is above it" for a diesel day
  tank).
- F-09 scope: the IEC 60204-1 page's abstract says it "applies to electrical, electronic and programmable electronic
  equipment and systems to machines not portable by hand while working". Lantern names it (and NFPA 79, industrial
  machinery) for any circuit -- a domestic well pump, a house's frost stat, a boiler's high limit. The rule holds; the
  code named may not be the one that governs that equipment. Not judged further: no page on the codes for boilers,
  wells or household controls was opened.
- No case: the reversing given's kept line reads "the overload OL1 on M1, OL1 on M2" (one overload listed twice).
- No case: Canada, "Canadian" and CSA are read as "US practice (NEC and NFPA 79)" (P-25, P-60, P-61 agree as the
  nearer of the two practices offered); the text names the NEC where Canada's code is the CEC.

======================================================================================================================
WHAT AGREES (276)
======================================================================================================================
- Right circuits left as written and drawn as written (115 of 145): alarms on high switches without a cut word, and
  lamps and horns on any high switch; plain cooling fan thermostats, fan limit, cut-in above cut-out; heater
  thermostats and boiler high limits written nc in every spelling tried (nc, N.C., normally closed, nc after the
  label), manual reset, over-temperature and overheat cut-outs on heaters, steam pressure limits; low water cut-offs
  in six spellings (LWCO, cutoff, cut off, loss of water, on a permit relay); freeze stats (freeze stat, freezestat,
  low limit, low temperature cut-out, low temp limit, on a permit relay); refrigeration HP and LP controls, dual
  high/low controls, cut-in/cut-out pairs either way (positive numbers), a walk-in cooler, pump-down, condenser fan
  cycling; well pumps (30/50, cut-in/out, cut-out alone, low pressure cut-off, loss of prime), booster with low
  suction and high discharge cut-outs and a break tank float, vacuum and jet pumps; air compressors (cut-out, cut-in
  and cut-out, lead and lag, high discharge temperature, a high pressure unloader); gas valve low and high gas
  pressure and air proving; fill floats (one, two, max level, overfill cut-off, upper limit, a fill valve, a transfer
  pump with dry run protection); sump floats (on/off, high/low, single, dry run, an ejector with an alarm relay);
  duplex lift stations (Lantern's floats, including nc and "trip" names); two stops, stop buttons in a dozen
  spellings, e-stops in four forms, a stop relay, one stop for two motors; interlocks written and forward/reverse.
- Wrong circuits caught (46 of the 49 W- cases that must go back; not: the two e-stop lines and W-coilnc-22b): a high cut-out written open
  and a low cut-out written nc, on a coil, a relay, a solenoid, an ISA tag (LSHH); a stop written as an
  open button beside a start, on one coil or two; "off" beside "on". The line handed back is exactly the right one
  where it can be predicted, and copied as it stands it builds and draws the contact right: curly quotes, the label
  before the ID, a numbered line, "no", "N.O.", "normally open" taken out, "nc", "N.C.", "normally closed" taken out,
  nc after the label, two problems at once. Copied from fixText with the full stop it puts after one problem
  (T-01..T-06), the same. One practice named, never two (T-07). The practice named follows the question (400 V ->
  IEC, 480 V and 60 Hz -> US) and the saved choice.
- pick(): 51 of 70: voltages and frequencies, NEC, NFPA 79, NEMA, IEC, BS 7671, AS/NZS, VDE, countries, US, U.S.,
  USA, "us" the pronoun in lower case, Georgia, French drain, 230 V either way, Indiana, Paris Texas, Mexico, both
  codes named -> the saved choice, a saved value that is no practice -> US.
- The view (V-01..V-15): the line in US and IEC with each kept item's reference, the button switching both ways and
  saving the choice, the choice followed by the next question that names neither code (what goes back to the model
  names IEC), a 400 V or 480 V question overriding it, Chat's own view showing it, a sheet shown as before, nothing
  kept -> no line, Lantern.store throwing on get and set or missing: builds, shows, switches, follows US.
- Module drops (D-01..D-04): without CODE_CHECKS_CONTROL, without CODE_CHECKS, without both: the page loads with no
  error, a circuit is drawn as 1.24.35 drew it, Chat's view works; every right circuit of the cases that builds is
  drawn identically with and without the two modules (plan.circuit and summary).
- The bench guard (G-01..G-05): L.aiAct.prompt(q) is identical with and without the code checks for all 150 set A and
  150 set B questions. Against 1.24.35 two prompts differ (make-control, make-control-b), and they are identical once
  GIVENS and GIVENS_CONTROL are taken out too: the change is the givens', not the checks'. 2,105 saved model replies
  with a MAKE block (every tests/fixtures/bench_run*.json, liftstation_1230/run_35b.json, review1_1256_setb.json)
  rebuilt: 21 made a control circuit and were checked, 0 are questioned by a code check (so none to list), their
  drawings are identical with and without the checks, and each overload named in their kept lines is drawn on that
  starter. Note: none of those 21 has a pressure, temperature or float switch, so the saved replies guard the stop
  and kept-list checks only, not the cut-out check.
- Lantern's own blocks (K-01..K-14, ST-01..ST-05): each built-in given (starter, reversing, sequence, delayed start,
  compressor, fill, fill with two floats, sump, sump with alarm; US and IEC questions) built as it stands passes;
  stations of one, two and three pumps are not sent back.
- The code's form (S-01..S-06): both modules ASCII only, parse as ES5 (acorn, ecmaVersion 5), no quote inside a regex
  literal; tests/regex_quotes.js and tests/pc_compat.js pass on this build; AI_CONTROL asks Lantern.codeChecks only if
  it is there, in a try; AI_ACTIONS runs each view tool in a try; Depends has no circle.
- The references (F-01..F-08): see below.

======================================================================================================================
PAGES OPENED (2026-11-24) AND WHAT EACH SAID
======================================================================================================================
All three were read through WebFetch, which returns a model's reading of the page (quotes asked for word for word),
not the raw page. curl to docinfofiles.nfpa.org was refused by the session's proxy (403), so the PDF itself could not
be downloaded.
1. https://standards.iteh.ai/catalog/standards/iec/ce9c4b09-1552-4cae-a57f-b1652e9052ea/iec-60204-1-2016
   IEC 60204-1:2016, Edition 6.0 (2016-10), contents: "7.3 Protection of motors against overheating", "9.3.2
   Exceeding operating limits", "9.3.4 Interlocks between different operations and for contrary motions", "9.4
   Control functions in the event of failure", "10.7 Emergency stop devices" (also 7.2 Overcurrent protection, 9.3.1
   Reclosing or resetting of an interlocking safeguard, 9.3.3 Operation of auxiliary functions, 9.3.5 Reverse current
   braking, 10.7.1 Location of emergency stop devices, 10.7.2 Types of emergency stop device). Scope (abstract):
   "applies to electrical, electronic and programmable electronic equipment and systems to machines not portable by
   hand while working, including a group of machines working together in a co-ordinated manner".
   -> Lantern's 7.3 (overload), 9.3.2 (cut-outs), 9.3.4 (interlocks), 9.4 (stops), 10.7 (emergency stop): each
      matches its title. AGREE (F-01..F-05).
2. https://www.ecmweb.com/maintenance-repair-operations/motors/article/21243401/nec-motors-part-3 ("NEC: Motors --
   Part 3"): "Art. 430, Part III provides the requirements for motor and branch-circuit overload protection"; names
   430.31, 430.32, 430.33; no NEC edition stated.
   -> Lantern's "NEC Article 430, Part III" for the overload on a motor starter: AGREE (F-06).
3. https://docinfofiles.nfpa.org/files/AboutTheCodes/79/79_F2023_EEI_AAA_FD_FRStatements.pdf (166,884 characters,
   read in two passes): First Revisions labelled "FR-nn-NFPA 79-2022", on public inputs against NFPA 79-2021 (the F2023
   cycle). "10.7.3 Emergency Stop Actuators. Actuators of emergency stop devices shall be colored RED." "10.7.4.3
   Disconnecting (isolating) electrical devices means as described in 5.2.2, where accessible to the operator, shall
   also be permitted to serve the function of emergency stop." Annex E table: "ESTOP Emergency Stop", "OL Overload
   Relay". The heading of 10.7 itself is not in the text; 9.3.2, 9.3.4 and 9.4 do not appear.
   -> Lantern's "NFPA 79, 10.7" for the emergency stop: supported by its subsections on emergency stop devices, its
      own title not seen. AGREE (F-07). The other NFPA 79 rules are named by subject only, with no number (F-08):
      AGREE -- none was on the page. The module header's "for the 2024 edition" fits the F2023 cycle; the page itself
      never says 2024.

======================================================================================================================
WHAT WAS NOT RUN OR NOT CHECKED
======================================================================================================================
- No model ran (no small model, no 35B): saved replies were replayed only, and they hold no control circuit with a
  process switch.
- The line and button under a drawing were checked in jsdom only, not looked at in a browser; how they look is Adam's.
- Not opened: Kuphaldt, Lessons In Industrial Instrumentation (named in the module header for a switch's normal
  state; it is not shown to the user or the model). No page on boiler, well-pump, refrigeration or household-control
  codes was opened.
- The trade facts behind the right circuits (frost stats make on fall, a refrigeration oil safety runs its timer while
  the oil pressure is low, a defrost termination stat in series with the heaters opens on rise, a booster's suction
  cut-out and a well's dry-well cut-off stop on low pressure, an unloader energised at cut-out) are the reviewer's
  knowledge of the trades, not read on a page in this session. Each case says why it is right; where a name is
  ambiguous the case asks only that Lantern leave it as written (rule 7), not that one reading is the law.
- npm test was not run (as asked). tests/code_checks_1236.js and tests/fixtures/givens_review_1236/ were not read.
